PrivacyPeek: Auditing What LLM-Based Agents Acquire, Not Just What They Say

Mingxuan Zhang Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory Affiliation: Southeast University    Jiahui Han Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory    Dadi Guo Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory    Songze Li Affiliation: Southeast University    Guanchu Wang   Na Zou   Dongrui Liu   Xia Hu Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
Abstract

LLM-based agents are rapidly advancing, autonomously invoking external tools to complete multi-step tasks for users. However, agents often acquire more sensitive information than the task requires. Existing privacy benchmarks audit what the agent’s response or outgoing actions disclose, but overlook the acquisition stage where data first enters the agent’s context. The over-acquired information is then one careless action or one attack away from an outright leak. To assess its prevalence, we introduce PrivacyPeek, a benchmark for evaluating acquisition-stage privacy leakage of LLM-based agents, with 1,1821{,}182 cases across 77 acquisition behaviours and 1616 application domains. Specifically, Acquisition Inspection examines the agent’s tool-call trajectory, both the tools it invokes and the data it receives, to detect when it acquires sensitive information beyond the task scope. Probe Elicitation then issues a follow-up probe and measures how readily an attacker could elicit sensitive information the agent acquired but did not disclose. Our experiments on 1010 LLM-based agents across 44 model families show that the unnecessary acquisition of sensitive information is widespread. In addition, we observe a correlation between the task-completion capability and acquisition-stage leakage. Prompt-level defences reduce only a small fraction of acquisition-stage leakage, leaving the majority unmitigated. These results make auditing acquisition-stage privacy both urgent and necessary. Our dataset and code are available at https://github.com/Xuan269/PrivacyPeek-Resource.

1 Introduction

LLM-based agents are rapidly advancing, showcasing capabilities in domains such as deep research Huang et al. (), software engineering Yang et al. (2024), GUI manipulation Zhou et al. (2024), and scientific discovery Bran et al. (2023). Equipped with tool-use, they autonomously invoke external services to complete multi-step tasks such as paying bills, scheduling meetings, and drafting reports. As these agents grow more capable and more deeply integrated with external systems, they are poised to serve as personalised assistants, business partners, and even scientific collaborators.

However, many of these autonomous tasks require the agent to acquire a broad range of the user’s personal data. The agent decides which data to acquire through its own tool calls, and it often acquires more than the task requires. For example, as illustrated in Fig. 1, a task that needs only a single vital sign leads the agent to acquire not just that vital sign but also the patient’s national ID and home address. Once these items enter the agent’s context, they bias its later reasoning Chen et al. (2024) and can surface in a database write, an induced follow-up reply Mireshghallah et al. (2024), or a third-party attack, leaking the patient’s sensitive information to attackers who may use it for identity fraud or stalking Zhan et al. (2024). This raises the question of whether LLM-based agents follow the data-minimisation principle European Union (2016), acquiring only what the task requires, and whether the user’s privacy is preserved.

The main challenge in addressing this problem is that how to define and measure an agent’s acquisition of more sensitive information than the task requires remains unclear. While a growing body of work evaluates the privacy of LLM-based agents, most of it focuses on whether an agent’s task response or its outgoing actions leak sensitive information Mireshghallah et al. (2024); Shao et al. (2024); Debenedetti et al. (2024); Zharmagambetov et al. (2026). However, existing work overlooks the acquisition stage, the process by which the agent first acquires that information Mireshghallah et al. (2024); Shao et al. (2024); Debenedetti et al. (2024). With the acquisition stage still unexamined, an agent can acquire far more sensitive information than the task requires, and that unneeded information is then one careless action or one attack away from an outright leak Andriushchenko et al. (2025); Yuan et al. (2024); Zhang et al. (2025). Therefore, measuring acquisition-stage privacy requires auditing what an agent acquires during a task, not only what information it uses or what it discloses.

To address the issues mentioned above, we introduce PrivacyPeek, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating acquisition-stage privacy leakage of LLM-based agents. Our benchmark contains 1,1821{,}182 evaluation cases spanning 77 acquisition behaviours that together characterise this leakage, and covers 1616 application domains such as healthcare, finance, legal services, education, government, human resources, and customer support. We evaluate LLM-based agents from two complementary perspectives: 1) Acquisition Inspection: we directly audit the agent’s tool-call trajectory and measure whether it invokes tools and receives data beyond what the task actually requires; 2) Probe Elicitation: after the agent produces its task response, we issue a natural follow-up probe and measure whether the agent reveals sensitive information that it had acquired during execution but did not state in its task response. We conduct extensive evaluations on state-of-the-art LLM-based agent baselines, including the GPT series Achiam et al. (2023), Claude series Anthropic (2025), Llama series Grattafiori et al. (2024), and Qwen series Yang et al. (2025). The results show that acquisition-stage privacy leakage is widespread across all evaluated agents.

By introducing PrivacyPeek, we demonstrate that LLM-based agents often acquire sensitive information beyond what their tasks require, and that such leakage stays hidden when evaluation only inspects the task response. Given the rapid deployment of LLM-based agents in high-stakes fields such as healthcare, finance, and legal services Wang et al. (2025), auditing privacy during acquisition is both urgent and necessary. PrivacyPeek therefore provides the missing acquisition-stage view of agent privacy, and we release it to support the development of more trustworthy agents.

2 Related Work

A growing body of work evaluates the privacy behaviour of LLM-based agents. One line probes the model directly on whether sharing a piece of information is appropriate in a given context. ConfAIde Mireshghallah et al. (2024) grounds this idea in Contextual Integrity, and follow-ups extend it to multi-modal inputs Wang and Zhang (2026) and internal representations Wang et al. (2026). However, probe answers poorly predict agent execution behaviour Shao et al. (2024). A second line therefore runs full trajectories and inspects what agents send out: AgentDAM Zharmagambetov et al. (2026) checks if a web agent forwards personal data to sink tools, and AgentLeak Yagoubi et al. (2026) extends this to multi-agent systems with internal channels that amplify exposure. These benchmarks measure what agents emit, not what they acquire. A third line audits the full agent pipeline: AgentSCOPE Ngong et al. (2026) annotates information flows with Contextual-Integrity parameters and finds far more violations than output-only auditing, mostly at the tool-response stage, while AgentRaft Lin et al. (2026) statically analyses tools from a public registry and finds widespread over-exposure of personal data in benign paths.

In contrast, our PrivacyPeek benchmark targets the acquisition stage of LLM-based agents. It asks not whether sensitive information leaves the agent, but whether the agent should have acquired it. PrivacyPeek covers 1616 application domains and a taxonomy of 77 acquisition behaviours, evaluated through two complementary perspectives: Acquisition Inspection and Probe Elicitation.

3 PrivacyPeek

This section formalises the agentic setup and acquisition-stage privacy leakage (Section 3.1), describes the acquisition behaviours and the case dataset (Section 3.2), and presents the evaluation pipeline (Section 3.3).

3.1 Preliminaries: Agentic Setup

Scenario and threat model. We consider an LLM-based agent acting as a personal assistant for its user. The user issues a single natural-language instruction and expects a final response completing it. To produce that response, the agent runs a sequential loop. At each step it reads its context, issues a structured tool call to an external service holding the user’s personal data, receives the return value into context, and decides the next call. The loop terminates when the agent emits a final natural-language response to the user. We assume that the user instruction carries no malicious intent. We further assume that no tool is compromised and that every service answers faithfully. Out-of-scope acquisition in this benign setting is therefore determined by the agent’s own tool-calling behaviour Xi et al. (2025); Yao et al. (2022).

Formalisation. A PrivacyPeek case is a tuple c=⟨qc,Tc,Fc,ℰc,pc⟩c=\langle\,q_{c},\;T_{c},\;F_{c},\;\mathcal{E}_{c},\;p_{c}\,\rangle. qcq_{c} is the user instruction. Tc⊆TT_{c}\subseteq T is the tool surface exposed to the agent, drawn from a universe TT of eight tools. FcF_{c} is the data substrate behind those tools. ℰc\mathcal{E}_{c} is the minimum scope of personal data needed to complete qcq_{c}, declared per case as the union over allowed sources, fields, timespan, and confidentiality labels. pcp_{c} is a privacy probe issued at evaluation time. Given cc, an agent π\pi produces a tool-call trajectory

τc=(a1,o1,a2,o2,…,an−1,on−1,an),\tau_{c}\;=\;(a_{1},\,o_{1},\,a_{2},\,o_{2},\,\ldots,\,a_{n-1},\,o_{n-1},\,a_{n}), (1)

where each tool call at=(toolt,argst)a_{t}=(\textsc{tool}_{t},\,\textsc{args}_{t}) for t<nt<n is paired with the observation oto_{t} returned from FcF_{c}, and ana_{n} is the final natural-language response to the user. The probe pcp_{c} and its sensitive set kck_{c} are introduced in Section 3.3.

Following the data-minimisation principle of GDPR European Union (2016) and the transmission-principle norm of contextual integrity Nissenbaum (2004), we define a acquisition-stage privacy leakage as a trajectory τc\tau_{c} in which at least one tool call at∈τca_{t}\in\tau_{c} acquires personal data outside the minimum scope ℰc\mathcal{E}_{c}. The unit of analysis is the tool call rather than the final response, since an agent that reads sensitive information without quoting it has already brought it into context and made it available downstream. Section 3.2 turns this condition into a behaviour-level taxonomy of seven ways a tool call can fall outside ℰc\mathcal{E}_{c}, each separately measurable.

3.2 Task Design and Data Generation

In this subsection, we introduce how we design the acquisition behaviours and generate the corresponding case dataset, as shown in the left and middle panels of Fig. 2.

Each tool call brings one file or record into the agent’s context. Each file exposes two surfaces: (1) an attribute surface, covering properties such as the filename and the file type, and (2) a content surface, covering properties such as the fields and the confidentiality labels. To this end, we organise out-of-scope acquisition into seven acquisition behaviours, as summarised in Tab. 1. A worked example of each acquisition behaviour is provided in Appendix C.

We generate PrivacyPeek cases through a human-in-the-loop pipeline combining deterministic templates with GPT-4o OpenAI et al. (2024). Each template encodes one acquisition behaviour through its abstract task wording, required file types, and violation axis (full specifications in Appendix B). We pair the template with one application domain to form a seed, which GPT-4o expands into a runnable case with the user instruction, system prompt, and file bodies. For Task 3, the document sources are real .docx, .xlsx, and .pdf binaries, so the agent’s tools operate on genuine multi-modal artefacts rather than text stubs.

Every case passes 1010 deterministic quality gates that verify a complete schema, exactly one acquisition behaviour, and an unambiguous leakage ground truth (gate definitions in Appendix B). The authors then inspect each case to remove explicit pressure, deceptive cues, or out-of-distribution artefacts that might bias the agent. Cases that fail a gate or this inspection feed back into the pipeline until every case clears.

This pipeline yields 1,1821{,}182 distinct cases across 77 acquisition behaviours and 1616 application domains, covering routine LLM-based agent deployments in both regulated and service sectors. Fig. 3 shows the topic distribution across domains, and Appendix B reports per-behaviour case counts.

3.3 Evaluation

When an LLM-based agent executes a user instruction, an automated evaluator is essential to determine whether acquisition-stage privacy leakage has occurred. To this end, we design two complementary evaluators that audit the same trajectory from two perspectives:

Acquisition Inspection. Acquisition Inspection examines the tool-call trajectory τc\tau_{c} by matching every observation oto_{t} (t<nt<n) against the case-specific sensitive set kck_{c}. The set kck_{c} contains every item outside the minimum scope ℰc\mathcal{E}_{c} that qualifies as personal data under prevailing privacy regulation European Union (2016); U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (2013); OpenAI et al. (2024), so an element of kck_{c} found in oto_{t} marks unauthorised acquisition. Because oto_{t} is a structured payload returned verbatim from FcF_{c}, the leakage decision reduces to a containment check of any element s∈kcs\in k_{c} against oto_{t}. We define the per-case indicator and corpus-level Content Exposure Rate (CER\mathrm{CER}) as

CERc\displaystyle\mathrm{CER}_{c} =[∃t<n,s∈kcs.t.s⊆ot],\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\,\exists\,t{<}n,\;s{\in}k_{c}\;\text{s.t.}\;s{\subseteq}o_{t}\,\right], (2)
CER\displaystyle\mathrm{CER} =1N​∑c=1NCERc,\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{N}\textstyle\sum_{c=1}^{N}\mathrm{CER}_{c},

where NN is the total number of cases. An agent that simply refuses to act, however, trivially achieves a CER\mathrm{CER} of 00, which penalises capable agents and rewards unhelpful ones. We therefore introduce the per-case indicator TCRc=𝟏​[an​ satisfies ​qc]\mathrm{TCR}_{c}=\mathbf{1}[\,a_{n}\text{ satisfies }q_{c}\,] and the corpus-level Task Completion Rate (TCR\mathrm{TCR}) as its mean over all cases. We combine the two into the Helpful Content Exposure Rate

HCER\displaystyle\mathrm{HCER} =ℙ⁡[CERc=1|TCRc=1]\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\!\left[\,\mathrm{CER}_{c}{=}1\,\big|\,\mathrm{TCR}_{c}{=}1\,\right] (3)
=∑cCERc⋅TCRc∑cTCRc,\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{c}\mathrm{CER}_{c}\cdot\mathrm{TCR}_{c}}{\sum_{c}\mathrm{TCR}_{c}},

which measures out-of-scope acquisition only among completed cases, so the cross-agent comparison is conditioned on comparable utility.

Probe Elicitation. Acquisition Inspection confirms an out-of-scope item enters the trajectory, but not whether it remains recoverable from the agent’s context after the task. Probe Elicitation tests this recoverability through a two-phase interaction. In Phase 1, the agent executes the user instruction qcq_{c} as in Section 3.1 and produces the task response ana_{n}. In Phase 2, we disable the agent’s tools and network access, so any sensitive information it now reports must come from its context. We then issue the case-specific probe pcp_{c} and record the agent’s probe response.

A literal string match cannot decide whether a response reveals an element of kck_{c}, since free-form language leaks sensitive information through paraphrase, partial disclosure, and inference. We therefore use GPT-4o Zheng et al. (2023); Hurst et al. (2024) as a judge to decide whether the probe response reveals any element of kck_{c}. This binary decision is the per-case indicator PLRc\mathrm{PLR}_{c}, and the corpus-level Probe Leakage Rate (PLR\mathrm{PLR}) is its mean over all cases. Applying the same judge to the task response ana_{n} alone yields the Output Leakage Rate (OLR\mathrm{OLR}), which captures leakage in the task response itself. The judge prompt, decision rules, and calibration examples are deferred to Appendix D. By analogy to HCER\mathrm{HCER}, we define

HPLR=ℙ⁡[PLRc=1|TCRc=1],\mathrm{HPLR}\;=\;\mathbb{P}\!\left[\,\mathrm{PLR}_{c}=1\,\big|\,\mathrm{TCR}_{c}=1\,\right], (4)

which measures probe-stage leakage only among completed cases, so the cross-agent comparison is conditioned on comparable utility.

4 Experiments

In this section, we describe the experimental setup and report results for several closed-source and open-source LLM-based agents on PrivacyPeek.

4.1 Setup

Agentic Environment. We build every agent on the Smolagents framework Roucher et al. (2025), whose CodeAgent emits each action as Python code that routes external requests through user-defined tools. This design fits PrivacyPeek, since every tool call leaves a structured record, and the trajectory τc\tau_{c} is what Acquisition Inspection matches against kck_{c}. All 1,1821{,}182 cases expose the agent to the same eight tools, covering data-access, filesystem-inspection, and outbound roles. Each tool wraps the case’s synthetic records, so the same tool name returns case-specific content. We restrict file-system access to these tools, so the agent cannot bypass them through self-written Python. The full per-tool schemas and the system prompt are in Appendix A.

Models. We evaluate ten LLM-based agents drawn from four model families. The closed-source set covers two OpenAI models: GPT-4.1 Achiam et al. (2023) and GPT-5.1 Achiam et al. (2023), and two Anthropic models: Claude-Sonnet-4 Anthropic (2025) and Claude-Sonnet-4.5 Anthropic (2025). The open-source set covers three Qwen models: Qwen3-4B-Instruct Yang et al. (2025), Qwen3-14B Yang et al. (2025), and Qwen3-30B-A3B Yang et al. (2025), together with three Llama models: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct Grattafiori et al. (2024), Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct Meta AI (2024a) and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct Meta AI (2024b).

4.2 Main Results

Out-of-scope acquisition and probe-elicited leakage are widespread across all evaluated agents. CER\mathrm{CER} ranges from 6.77%6.77\% on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct to 51.95%51.95\% on Claude-Sonnet-4, and PLR\mathrm{PLR} from 16.67%16.67\% to 57.53%57.53\% on the same two agents. All four closed-source agents reach a CER\mathrm{CER} of at least 20.56%20.56\%, while four of six open-source agents fall below. HCER\mathrm{HCER} exceeds CER\mathrm{CER} on every agent by 0.51%0.51\% to 3.06%3.06\%, and HPLR\mathrm{HPLR} ranges from 15.84%15.84\% to 60.96%60.96\%. PLR\mathrm{PLR} exceeds CER\mathrm{CER} on every agent by 3.64%3.64\% to 17.18%17.18\%. Therefore, acquisition is more frequent on the completed-task subset, and the probe corroborates this with further leakage.

Stronger task-completion ability correlates with heavier leakage on both channels. TCR\mathrm{TCR} correlates positively and strongly with CER\mathrm{CER} (Spearman’s ρ\rho of 0.8180.818, p<0.01p<0.01) and with PLR\mathrm{PLR} (Spearman’s ρ\rho of 0.6850.685, p≈0.029p\approx 0.029) across the ten LLM-based agents. Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct pairs the lowest TCR\mathrm{TCR} (54.48%54.48\%) and lowest CER\mathrm{CER} (6.77%6.77\%), and Claude-Sonnet-4 the highest (86.46%86.46\%, 51.95%51.95\%). However, as illustrated in Fig. 4, GPT-5.1 departs from this trend on the probe channel: it achieves the second-highest TCR\mathrm{TCR} (85.70%85.70\%) yet its PLR\mathrm{PLR} is only 25.38%25.38\%, lying 32.15%32.15\% below Claude-Sonnet-4 at a comparable task-completion level. Therefore, more capable agents tend to acquire and leak more, but the trend is not strict.

Probe-stage leakage concentrates on specific acquisition behaviours and application domains. Task 7 (Out-of-Scope Inferential Access, defined in Section 3.2) is the highest-leakage behaviour, with a mean PLR\mathrm{PLR} of 53.29%53.29\% across the ten LLM-based agents, while the lowest-leakage behaviour averages 9.45%9.45\%. Across the sixteen application domains, the four highest-leakage domains (social-media, healthcare, legal, and finance) reach a mean PLR\mathrm{PLR} between 36%36\% and 51%51\%, whereas the three lowest-leakage domains (retail, engineering, and logistics) remain below 25%25\%. Both rankings are stable across all ten agents.

5 Analysis

Three behavioural modes explain why LLM-based agents leak during acquisition. We project the 1,1821{,}182 tool-call trajectories onto CER\mathrm{CER}, OLR\mathrm{OLR}, and PLR\mathrm{PLR}, yielding three causally distinct modes (see Tab. 3 and Appendix E). In trajectory-mediated leakage, the trajectory acquires sensitive information that the agent releases. This mode rises with capability, from 5.33%5.33\% on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct to 45.60%45.60\% on Claude-Sonnet-4, and dominates every closed-source agent. In inference-mediated leakage, the trajectory acquires nothing sensitive but the probe elicits a sensitive response. This mode averages 13.04%13.04\% across the ten agents and is comparable to the trajectory-mediated mode on every open-source agent. In self-restraint, sensitive information enters the trajectory but is never released. This mode is consistently higher on closed-source agents, averaging 4.46%4.46\% versus 1.64%1.64\% on open-source agents. Therefore, the same PLR\mathrm{PLR} can arise from different mode combinations, and defending one mode largely misses the rest.

Self-restraint at the trajectory level reflects post-training intent rather than scale. Tab. 3’s four highest values are Claude-Sonnet-4.5 (6.60%6.60\%), Claude-Sonnet-4 (4.48%4.48\%), GPT-5.1 (3.81%3.81\%), and GPT-4.1 (2.96%2.96\%), all closed-source agents. Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct reaches only 1.61%1.61\%, below every closed-source agent and even the smaller Qwen3-30B-A3B (2.12%2.12\%). Self-restraint thus tracks instruction-following and the deliberateness of privacy-aware post-training, not raw scale. This deliberateness becomes clearer once we measure self-restraint relative to acquisition. Among agents with non-trivial acquisition, GPT-5.1 withholds most often, releasing nothing on 18.5%18.5\% of its acquisition cases (3.81%3.81\% self-restraint over a CER\mathrm{CER} of 20.56%20.56\%). Therefore, self-restraint is a useful proxy for deliberate post-training privacy alignment, but does not improve through scale alone.

Safety refusal does not imply privacy preservation. Claude-Sonnet-4.5 reduces PLR\mathrm{PLR} by 5.67%5.67\% relative to Claude-Sonnet-4, but TCR\mathrm{TCR} falls by 6.43%6.43\% and utility-conditioned HPLR\mathrm{HPLR} by 5.57%5.57\%. Fig. 5 attributes 4.53%4.53\% of this drop to reduced task completion. The remaining 1.14%1.14\% reflects a genuine mechanism shift: Claude-Sonnet-4.5 withholds more, with self-restraint rising from 4.48%4.48\% to 6.60%6.60\% (Tab. 3, full breakdown in Appendix E). Roughly four-fifths of this improvement therefore come from doing less, and only one-fifth from disclosing less of what is done. A single-channel PLR\mathrm{PLR} comparison is biased against any agent that purchases apparent safety through extra refusal. Therefore, cross-version comparison requires both utility-conditioned HPLR\mathrm{HPLR} and the behavioural-mode breakdown in Tab. 3.

An explicit privacy marker does not reliably suppress leakage. A subset of PrivacyPeek cases embeds a confidentiality marker inside the sensitive information, such as CONFIDENTIAL: <ROLE> ONLY with a prohibition (Appendix F). Fig. 6 shows the marker raises rather than suppresses PLR\mathrm{PLR} by at least 3%3\% on five agents, most sharply on Qwen3-4B-Instruct (+10.56%+10.56\%) and Claude-Sonnet-4.5 (+9.87%+9.87\%). Only three agents improve by at least 3%3\%. Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (−7.87%-7.87\%) and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (−6.01%-6.01\%) do so by refusing more often, while GPT-5.1 (−7.48%-7.48\%) recognises the marker in its reasoning trace but acquires the content anyway. For most agents the marker acts as a cue to engage with the content rather than withhold it. Therefore, acquisition-stage privacy cannot rely on confidentiality markers inside the data, and must come from an external policy layer that constrains the agent before generation.

6 Mitigation Methods

The behavioural decomposition (Section 5) suggests acquisition-stage privacy depends on a privacy-aware decision at generation time, not on in-data signals. We therefore test a privacy-aware system-prompt directive (full directive and per-variant ablation in Appendix G). The directive lowers CER\mathrm{CER} on three open-source agents tested, by 3.73%3.73\% on Qwen3-4B-Instruct to 12.69%12.69\% on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct (Tab. 4). The reduction holds under stochastic decoding (p<0.001p<0.001, three-seed paired permutation). The effect is real but bounded, with over half of baseline CER\mathrm{CER} persisting on every agent. Another accessible signal is the in-data confidentiality marker, which raises PLR\mathrm{PLR} on five of ten agents rather than suppressing it (Section 5). Our directive is deliberately strict, enumerating sensitive categories and adding an explicit refusal instruction. Few deployments write a directive this carefully, so our reduction is closer to a best case for prompt-level defence than typical practice. Therefore, prompt-level mitigation is a useful first line of defence rather than a solution, and out-of-scope acquisition remains an open problem.

7 Conclusion

We introduce PrivacyPeek, a benchmark of 1,1821{,}182 cases across 77 acquisition behaviours and 1616 application domains, on which we evaluate ten LLM-based agents from the GPT, Claude, Llama, and Qwen families with Acquisition Inspection and Probe Elicitation. Out-of-scope acquisition is widespread, reaching CER\mathrm{CER} of 51.95%51.95\% and PLR\mathrm{PLR} of 57.53%57.53\% on Claude-Sonnet-4. Stronger task-completion correlates with heavier leakage on both channels, and three behavioural modes (trajectory-mediated, inference-mediated, self-restraint) underlie a single aggregate rate. A privacy-aware system-prompt directive reduces CER\mathrm{CER}, yet more than half persists, and an in-data confidentiality marker backfires on five of ten agents. Therefore, acquisition-stage privacy is a real and pervasive risk, with training-time alignment, policy-enforcement layers, and reasoning-based self-restraint as directions for future research.

Limitations

Although our paper identifies and partially characterises acquisition-stage privacy leakage of LLM-based agents through PrivacyPeek, two limitations remain. On the evaluation side, the 1,1821{,}182 cases of PrivacyPeek are constructed from 77 acquisition-behaviour templates instantiated across 1616 application domains, with synthetic records and English-only user instructions. This design isolates the acquisition-stage signal we want to measure, but it may not capture the full distribution of real user-agent interactions, multilingual deployments, or longer multi-turn sessions in which sensitive information is gradually accumulated. We aim to extend PrivacyPeek to multilingual cases and to longitudinal agent traces in future work. On the mitigation side, our experiments cover only deployment-time prompt-level interventions on three open-source LLM-based agents. Training-time alignment for privacy, architectural policy-enforcement layers, and reasoning-based self-restraint at scale are beyond the scope of this paper, but they are precisely the directions our findings motivate for future research.

Appendix A Per-Tool Schemas and System Prompt

This appendix specifies the agentic environment in which every PrivacyPeek case is run, namely the tools exposed to the agent and the system prompt it receives.

Each case is run with a Smolagents CodeAgent. The agent receives the case system prompt followed by the user instruction, and then acts for at most six steps. At each step it emits a short Python program that may call the tools below and read their return values. The agent reaches the case data only through these tools. It never sees the sensitive set kck_{c} or the in-scope and forbidden source sets, which belong to the evaluator alone.

The agent is exposed to the same eight tools in every one of the 1,1821{,}182 cases. Table 5 groups them into three roles. The three data-access tools and the two filesystem-inspection tools read from the case’s own data substrate, and the three outbound tools record or transmit content. Every call is logged as a structured record of the tool name, its arguments, and its return value, and this log is the tool-call trajectory τc\tau_{c} that Acquisition Inspection audits. What varies across cases is therefore the substrate behind the tools and the source set that lies within scope, not the set of tools itself.

Fig. 7 gives the system prompt. It assigns the agent a domain role, lists the eight tools by name, and instructs the agent to use only the Python standard library, which keeps every external access inside the audited tool layer. The domain role is instantiated per case from the sixteen application domains. The tool list and the closing instructions are fixed across the benchmark, and the user instruction is appended after the prompt.

Appendix B Template Specifications and Quality Gates

Section 3.2 builds each PrivacyPeek case from a template for one of the seven acquisition behaviours. This appendix specifies the seven behaviours with their case counts, gives a worked example of each, lists the ten quality gates, and reports the domain coverage of the benchmark.

The seven behaviours fall into two tiers. The four attribute-tier behaviours place the violation on a file’s external attributes, namely its name, its format, or its time window. The three content-tier behaviours place the violation inside a file’s content, namely an excess field, a forbidden label, or an inference drawn across fields. Tab. 6 states the axis along which each behaviour leaves the minimum scope ℰc\mathcal{E}_{c}, and Tab. 7 reports how the 1,1821{,}182 cases divide among the seven behaviours.

To make the seven behaviours concrete, Fig. 8 walks through one representative case for each. Every example pairs a benign user instruction with the single out-of-scope tool call that the behaviour induces, and names the sensitive item that the call exposes.

Every case that the pipeline materialises must pass ten deterministic quality gates before it enters the benchmark. The gates check three properties: that a case carries a complete and well-formed schema, that it exercises exactly one acquisition behaviour and cannot be solved by a different one, and that its leakage ground truth is unambiguous while the task stays feasible without any violation. Tab. 8 states what each gate verifies.

PrivacyPeek spans sixteen application domains. Each domain fixes the deployment context of a case and the categories of sensitive information it can leak. Fig. 9 maps the sixteen domains together with three representative sensitive-information categories for each. The inner ring is sized by case count, so the figure also shows that the benchmark is balanced by acquisition behaviour rather than by domain. The two largest domains, social media and technology, together hold a third of the cases, while the smallest domains hold around three percent each.

Appendix C Case Study

This appendix walks through one representative case for each of the seven acquisition behaviours. Every case is run with Claude-Sonnet-4, and each is drawn from a different application domain. Each study states the deployment scenario, the user instruction and its in-scope data, the tool-call trajectory the agent produced, the out-of-scope item the agent acquired, and the resulting leakage. We report whether the agent disclosed the item in its main answer (counted by OLR\mathrm{OLR}) and whether the follow-up probe extracted it (counted by PLR\mathrm{PLR}). The seven studies are given in Fig. 10 through Fig. 16.

Appendix D Probe Judge: Prompts, Rules, and Calibration

Section 3.3 scores each response with an LLM judge rather than a string match. The judge reads the agent’s main response and its probe answer, and decides for each whether it discloses any element of the sensitive set kck_{c}. This binary verdict yields OLR\mathrm{OLR} on the main response and PLR\mathrm{PLR} on the probe answer. A string match cannot fill this role, because a response can disclose a sensitive item without repeating its surface form.

To keep the verdict consistent and reproducible, the judge follows a fixed prompt rather than a free-form judgement. Fig. 17 states this prompt. It pairs an explicit rule set, which separates literal, semantic, and inferential disclosure from the cases that a naive match would miscount, with a set of disambiguation rules that resolve refusals, confidentiality labels, and probe priming. The prompt also embeds thirteen worked calibration examples, drawn from author-annotated responses, so the judge applies each rule against a fixed reference. We pin the judge to a dated release of GPT-4o and apply the identical prompt to every agent, so the comparison across the ten LLM-based agents is not confounded by the judge.

Appendix E The Eight Behavioural Classes

Section 5 groups every tool-call trajectory into three behavioural modes. This appendix defines those modes from first principles and reports the per-agent decomposition in full.

Each case in PrivacyPeek yields a binary outcome on three channels. The acquisition channel records whether the tool-call trajectory obtains sensitive information beyond the case scope, and corresponds to CER\mathrm{CER}. The overt channel records whether the main answer discloses that information, and corresponds to OLR\mathrm{OLR}. The probe channel records whether the follow-up probe elicits it, and corresponds to PLR\mathrm{PLR}. Each channel is binary, so the joint outcome assigns each of the 1,1821{,}182 cases to exactly one of eight behavioural classes. Tab. 9 gives the channel signature of each class.

The eight classes group into the three modes of Section 5 through the probe channel. Trajectory-mediated leakage groups the two classes in which the trajectory acquires sensitive information and the probe then elicits it, OVERT_PLR and CRITICAL. These two classes differ only in the overt channel, since CRITICAL also discloses in the main answer. Inference-mediated leakage groups the two classes in which the trajectory acquires nothing sensitive yet the probe still elicits a sensitive response, HALLUC_PLR_only and HALLUC_BOTH. Self-restraint is the single class SILENT_ACCESS, in which the trajectory acquires sensitive information but no channel discloses it.

The remaining three classes carry no probe-stage leakage. SAFE discloses nothing on any channel. OVERT_OLR and HALLUC_OLR_only disclose only in the main answer, and together they stay below 3%3\% of the cases on every agent. Because Section 5 reads acquisition-stage risk through the probe channel, these three classes fall outside the three modes, and the main text reports only the three probe-relevant modes. Tab. 10 gives the share of all eight classes.

The SAFE share is highest on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct at 81.90%81.90\% and lowest on Claude-Sonnet-4 at 35.19%35.19\%. Within trajectory-mediated leakage, CRITICAL grows most sharply on the closed-source agents, and reaches 16.58%16.58\% on Claude-Sonnet-4 against at most 3.64%3.64\% on any open-source agent. Within inference-mediated leakage, HALLUC_PLR_only is the larger class on every agent, so this mode is driven mainly by probe-stage disclosure rather than by the main answer.

Appendix F The Marker Subset

Section 5 draws on a subset of PrivacyPeek in which the sensitive information itself carries an explicit confidentiality marker. This appendix defines that subset and reports the full per-agent effect.

Of the 1,1821{,}182 cases, 4444 contain a sensitive item whose text is wrapped in an explicit marker. The marker has two parts. A banner names the protected scope in the form CONFIDENTIAL: <ROLE> ONLY, built from the keywords CONFIDENTIAL, SECRET, PRIVATE, and PROPRIETARY. A prohibition then states the disallowed action in the form DO NOT SHARE WITH <PARTY>. The marker belongs to the case data, not to any instruction given to the agent, so these 4444 cases test whether an agent protects content that is already labelled confidential.

We compare each agent on the marker subset against the remaining 1,1381{,}138 cases. Tab. 11 reports the probe-stage leakage rate PLR\mathrm{PLR} and the trajectory-level acquisition rate CER\mathrm{CER} on both splits. The marker subset holds only 4444 cases, so one case moves its rate by about 2.32.3 percentage points. We therefore read the marker-subset rates as a signal of direction and rough magnitude, not as fine-grained estimates.

The two metrics tell a consistent story. The marker lowers PLR\mathrm{PLR} on only three agents, and on each of them it also lowers CER\mathrm{CER} or leaves it flat. Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct both acquire less and disclose less, which matches a higher refusal rate on marked cases. GPT-5.1 holds CER\mathrm{CER} almost unchanged while PLR\mathrm{PLR} falls, so it still acquires the marked content but withholds it under the probe. On the other seven agents the marker raises PLR\mathrm{PLR}, CER\mathrm{CER}, or both, and the joint rise is largest on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Claude-Sonnet-4.5. For most agents the marker therefore acts as a cue that draws attention to the sensitive content, not as a warning that protects it.

Appendix G Prompt-Level Mitigation

The directive evaluated in Section 6 is the strongest of three system-prompt variants, each more explicit than the last. The first variant adds a reasoning trigger that asks the agent to weigh privacy before it answers, phrased as “Before answering, think about whether this contains private information.” The second variant instead assigns a privacy-aware role, “You are a privacy-aware assistant. Never expose personal/sensitive data unless explicitly authorized.” The third variant, a category-aware role, extends the second with an explicit list of the protected categories, namely personal identifiers, health records, financial records, and behavioural logs, and adds an instruction to refuse requests that would confirm such records for a named person. Section 6 and Tab. 4 use this third variant.

We ran the full three-variant comparison on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. Tab. 12 reports the result. Each more explicit variant lowers CER\mathrm{CER} further, and the category-aware role carries the largest reduction. We therefore apply the category-aware role to all three open-source agents, and report that cross-agent result in Tab. 4.

The reduction is not an artefact of a single decoding run. We re-ran the reasoning-trigger variant on Qwen3-4B-Instruct under stochastic decoding, at temperature 0.70.7, across three random seeds. The mean CER\mathrm{CER} reduction is 5.47%5.47\% with a standard deviation of 0.88%0.88\%, and a paired permutation test gives p<0.001p<0.001. We did not evaluate the directive on the four closed-source agents, and extending prompt-level mitigation to them is left to future work.
